messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 68
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Psychologist
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 61

He first mentioned the abuse almost as an afterthought, in the third session, while we were discussing the arc of his career. He had been a clinical psychologist for over forty years, specializing in trauma. He knew the literature, the assessments, the therapeutic frameworks. He could describe the neurobiology of fear conditioning with the ease of someone reciting a favorite poem. And then, in the middle of explaining how he used to teach a graduate seminar on intimate partner violence, he paused. “I suppose I should tell you,” he said, looking at the floor, “that I know what it feels like from the other side now.”

The relationship began when he was fifty-two. She was a colleague, a fellow psychologist, brilliant and charismatic. He had been married for decades, but that marriage was quiet, safe, and he mistook her intensity for passion. They had a secret affair for two years before he left his wife. He moved into her apartment, full of hope and a fragile sense of new beginning. The first time she hit him, they had been living together for six months. It was over something trivial—a misplaced set of keys. She slapped him across the face, hard, and then immediately dissolved into tears, apologizing, saying she had never done anything like that before, that her own history of abuse had triggered her. He believed her. He was a psychologist. He understood.

The violence escalated slowly, in the way that is almost invisible when you are inside it. Pushing became shoving, shoving became grabbing by the collar, grabbing became punches to the ribs when he tried to leave the room. He never fought back. He would stand still and absorb it, his mind running a clinical commentary: *This is a trauma reenactment. She is dissociating. This is not about me.* He told himself he could help her. He was trained for this. And he was too ashamed to tell anyone—not his adult children, not his colleagues, not his own therapist, whom he stopped seeing because he could not bear to admit what was happening.

The end came three years ago, when she threw a glass paperweight at his head during an argument about money. He ducked, and it shattered against the wall. The next morning, he packed a bag and left while she was at work. He filed for divorce. She contested it viciously, accusing him of being the aggressor. He never reported the abuse to the police. He told himself it was because he could not prove it, but the deeper truth is that he could not bear the scrutiny, the pity, the possibility that his colleagues would see him as a victim.

Now, at sixty-eight, he has retired from practice. He lives alone in a small apartment. His second wife remarried quickly, and he has minimal contact with her. He sees his adult children on holidays, but he feels a wall between them—they do not know why their father’s new marriage ended, and he cannot bring himself to tell them. He spends his days reading, watching old films, and walking the same two-mile loop along the river. He still thinks like a psychologist: he can name every symptom. The hypervigilance that makes him flinch when a door opens. The intrusive images of her face, twisted in rage, that flash into his mind while he is trying to fall asleep. The way his heart pounds if he hears a raised voice in a café. He knows the PCL-5 was 61. He knows he meets criteria. He knows the exposure protocols. But when I ask him what he is afraid will happen if he allows himself to feel the terror he felt in those moments, he looks at me with the exhaustion of a man who has been both the healer and the wounded, and says, very quietly, “I’m afraid I will never stop feeling it.”
